arXiv:1007.1727v3 [physics.data-an] 24 Jun 2013

Asymptotic formulae for likelihood-based tests of new physics

Glen Cowan1, Kyle Cranmer2, Eilam Gross3, Ofer Vitells3

1 Physics Department, Royal Holloway, University of London, Egham, TW20 0EX, U.K.
2 Physics Department, New York University, New York, NY 10003, U.S.A.
3 Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot 76100, Israel

Keywords: systematic uncertainties, profile likelihood, hypothesis test, confidence interval, frequentist methods, asymptotic methods

Abstract

We describe likelihood-based statistical tests for use in high energy physics for the discovery of new phenomena and for construction of confidence intervals on model parameters.  We focus on the properties of the test procedures that allow one to account for systematic uncertainties. Explicit formulae for the asymptotic distributions of test statistics are derived using results of Wilks and Wald. We motivate and justify the use of a representative data set, called the “Asimov data set”, which provides a simple method to obtain the median experimental sensitivity of a search or measurement as well as fluctuations about this expectation.

1 Introduction

In particle physics experiments one often searches for processes that have been predicted but not yet seen, such as production of a Higgs boson. The statistical significance of an observed signal can be quantified by means of a pp-value or its equivalent Gaussian significance (discussed below). It is useful to characterize the sensitivity of an experiment by reporting the expected (e.g., mean or median) significance that one would obtain for a variety of signal hypotheses.

Finding both the significance for a specific data set and the expected significance can involve Monte Carlo calculations that are computationally expensive. In this paper we investigate approximate methods based on results due to Wilks [1] and Wald [2] by which one can obtain both the significance for given data as well as the full sampling distribution of the significance under the hypothesis of different signal models, all without recourse to Monte Carlo. In this way one can find, for example, the median significance and also a measure of how much one would expect this to vary as a result of statistical fluctuations in the data.

A useful element of the method involves estimation of the median significance by replacing the ensemble of simulated data sets by a single representative one, referred to here as the ‘‘Asimov’’ data set.11 1 The name of the Asimov data set is inspired by the short story Franchise, by Isaac Asimov [3]. In it, elections are held by selecting the single most representative voter to replace the entire electorate. In the past, this method has been used and justified intuitively (e.g., [4, 5]). Here we provide a formal mathematical justification for the method, explore its limitations, and point out several additional aspects of its use.

The present paper extends what was shown in Ref. [5] by giving more accurate formulas for exclusion significance and also by providing a quantitative measure of the statistical fluctuations in discovery significance and exclusion limits. For completeness some of the background material from [5] is summarized here.

In Sec. 2 the formalism of a search as a statistical test is outlined and the concepts of statistical significance and sensitivity are given precise definitions. Several test statistics based on the profile likelihood ratio are defined.

In Sec. 3, we use the approximations due to Wilks and Wald to find the sampling distributions of the test statistics and from these find pp-values and related quantities for a given data sample. In Sec. 4 we discuss how to determine the median significance that one would obtain for an assumed signal strength. Several example applications are shown in Sec. 5, and numerical implementation of the methods in the RooStats package is described in Sec. 6. Conclusions are given in Sec. 7.

2 Formalism of a search as a statistical test

In this section we outline the general procedure used to search for a new phenomenon in the context of a frequentist statistical test. For purposes of discovering a new signal process, one defines the null hypothesis, H0H_{0}, as describing only known processes, here designated as background. This is to be tested against the alternative H1H_{1}, which includes both background as well as the sought after signal. When setting limits, the model with signal plus background plays the role of H0H_{0}, which is tested against the background-only hypothesis, H1H_{1}.

To summarize the outcome of such a search one quantifies the level of agreement of the observed data with a given hypothesis HH by computing a pp-value, i.e., a probability, under assumption of HH, of finding data of equal or greater incompatibility with the predictions of HH. The measure of incompatibility can be based, for example, on the number of events found in designated regions of certain distributions or on the corresponding likelihood ratio for signal and background. One can regard the hypothesis as excluded if its pp-value is observed below a specified threshold.

In particle physics one usually converts the pp-value into an equivalent significance, ZZ, defined such that a Gaussian distributed variable found ZZ standard deviations above22 2 Some authors, e.g., Ref. [6], have defined this relation using a two-sided fluctuation of a Gaussian variable, with a 5​σ5\sigma significance corresponding to p=5.7×10−7p=5.7\times 10^{-7}. We take the one-sided definition above as this gives Z=0Z=0 for p=0.5p=0.5. its mean has an upper-tail probability equal to pp. That is,

Z=Φ−1​(1−p),Z=\Phi^{-1}(1-p)\,, (1)

where Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is the quantile (inverse of the cumulative distribution) of the standard Gaussian. For a signal process such as the Higgs boson, the particle physics community has tended to regard rejection of the background hypothesis with a significance of at least Z=5Z=5 as an appropriate level to constitute a discovery. This corresponds to p=2.87×10−7p=2.87\times 10^{-7}. For purposes of excluding a signal hypothesis, a threshold pp-value of 0.05 (i.e., 95% confidence level) is often used, which corresponds to Z=1.64Z=1.64.

It should be emphasized that in an actual scientific context, rejecting the background-only hypothesis in a statistical sense is only part of discovering a new phenomenon. One’s degree of belief that a new process is present will depend in general on other factors as well, such as the plausibility of the new signal hypothesis and the degree to which it can describe the data. Here, however, we only consider the task of determining the pp-value of the background-only hypothesis; if it is found below a specified threshold, we regard this as “discovery”.

It is often useful to quantify the sensitivity of an experiment by reporting the expected significance one would obtain with a given measurement under the assumption of various hypotheses. For example, the sensitivity to discovery of a given signal process H1H_{1} could be characterized by the expectation value, under the assumption of H1H_{1}, of the value of ZZ obtained from a test of H0H_{0}. This would not be the same as the ZZ obtained using Eq. (1) with the expectation of the pp-value, however, because the relation between ZZ and pp is nonlinear. The median ZZ and pp will, however, satisfy Eq. (1) because this is a monotonic relation. Therefore in the following we will take the term ‘expected significance’ always to refer to the median.

A widely used procedure to establish discovery (or exclusion) in particle physics is based on a frequentist significance test using a likelihood ratio as a test statistic. In addition to parameters of interest such as the rate (cross section) of the signal process, the signal and background models will contain in general nuisance parameters whose values are not taken as known a priori but rather must be fitted from the data.

It is assumed that the parametric model is sufficiently flexible so that for some value of the parameters it can be regarded as true. The additional flexibility introduced to parametrize systematic effects results, as it should, in a loss in sensitivity. To the degree that the model is not able to reflect the truth accurately, an additional systematic uncertainty will be present that is not quantified by the statistical method presented here.

To illustrate the use of the profile likelihood ratio, consider an experiment where for each selected event one measures the values of certain kinematic variables, and thus the resulting data can be represented as one or more histograms. Using the method in an unbinned analysis is a straightforward extension.

Suppose for each event in the signal sample one measures a variable xx and uses these values to construct a histogram 𝐧=(n1,…,nN)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf n$}}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{N}). The expectation value of nin_{i} can be written

E⁡[ni]=μ​si+bi,E[n_{i}]=\mu s_{i}+b_{i}\;, (2)

where the mean number of entries in the iith bin from signal and background are

si=stot​∫bin​ifs​(x,𝜽s)​𝑑x,\displaystyle s_{i}=s_{\rm tot}\int_{{\rm bin}\,i}f_{s}(x;\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{s})\,dx\,, (3)
bi=btot​∫bin​ifb​(x,𝜽b)​𝑑x.\displaystyle b_{i}=b_{\rm tot}\int_{{\rm bin}\,i}f_{b}(x;\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{b})\,dx\,. (4)

Here the parameter μ\mu determines the strength of the signal process, with μ=0\mu=0 corresponding to the background-only hypothesis and μ=1\mu=1 being the nominal signal hypothesis. The functions fs​(x,𝜽s)f_{s}(x;\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{s}) and fb​(x,𝜽b)f_{b}(x;\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{b}) are the probability density functions (pdfs) of the variable xx for signal and background events, and 𝜽s\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{s} and 𝜽b\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{b} represent parameters that characterize the shapes of pdfs. The quantities stots_{\rm tot} and btotb_{\rm tot} are the total mean numbers of signal and background events, and the integrals in (3) and (4) represent the probabilities for an event to be found in bin ii. Below we will use 𝜽=(𝜽s,𝜽b,btot)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}=(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{s},\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{b},b_{\rm tot}) to denote all of the nuisance parameters. The signal normalization stots_{\rm tot} is not, however, an adjustable parameter but rather is fixed to the value predicted by the nominal signal model.

In addition to the measured histogram 𝐧\textstyle\bf n one often makes further subsidiary measurements that help constrain the nuisance parameters. For example, one may select a control sample where one expects mainly background events and from them construct a histogram of some chosen kinematic variable. This then gives a set of values 𝐦=(m1,…,mM)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf m$}}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{M}) for the number of entries in each of the MM bins. The expectation value of mim_{i} can be written

E⁡[mi]=ui​(𝜽),E[m_{i}]=u_{i}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\;, (5)

where the uiu_{i} are calculable quantities depending on the parameters 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta. One often constructs this measurement so as to provide information on the background normalization parameter btotb_{\rm tot} and also possibly on the signal and background shape parameters.

The likelihood function is the product of Poisson probabilities for all bins:

L⁡(μ,𝜽)=∏j=1N(μ​sj+bj)njnj!​e−(μ​sj+bj)​∏k=1Mukmkmk!​e−uk.L(\mu,\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{(\mu s_{j}+b_{j})^{n_{j}}}{n_{j}!}e^{-(\mu s_{j}+b_{j})}\;\;\prod_{k=1}^{M}\frac{u_{k}^{m_{k}}}{m_{k}!}\,e^{-u_{k}}\;. (6)

To test a hypothesized value of μ\mu we consider the profile likelihood ratio

λ⁡(μ)=L⁡(μ,𝜽^^)L⁡(μ^,𝜽^).\lambda(\mu)=\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}})}{L(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}})}\;. (7)

Here 𝜽^^\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}} in the numerator denotes the value of 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta that maximizes LL for the specified μ\mu, i.e., it is the conditional maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator of 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta (and thus is a function of μ\mu). The denominator is the maximized (unconditional) likelihood function, i.e., μ^\hat{\mu} and 𝜽^\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}} are their ML estimators. The presence of the nuisance parameters broadens the profile likelihood as a function of μ\mu relative to what one would have if their values were fixed. This reflects the loss of information about μ\mu due to the systematic uncertainties.

In many analyses, the contribution of the signal process to the mean number of events is assumed to be non-negative. This condition effectively implies that any physical estimator for μ\mu must be non-negative. Even if we regard this to be the case, however, it is convenient to define an effective estimator μ^\hat{\mu} as the value of μ\mu that maximizes the likelihood, even this gives μ^<0\hat{\mu}<0 (but providing that the Poisson mean values, μ​si+bi\mu s_{i}+b_{i}, remain nonnegative). This will allow us in Sec. 3.1 to model μ^\hat{\mu} as a Gaussian distributed variable, and in this way we can determine the distributions of the test statistics that we consider. Therefore in the following we will always regard μ^\hat{\mu} as an effective estimator which is allowed to take on negative values.

2.1 Test statistic tμ=−2​ln⁡λ⁡(μ)t_{\mu}=-2\ln\lambda(\mu)

From the definition of λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) in Eq. (7), one can see that 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1, with λ\lambda near 1 implying good agreement between the data and the hypothesized value of μ\mu. Equivalently it is convenient to use the statistic

tμ=−2​ln⁡λ⁡(μ)t_{\mu}=-2\ln\lambda(\mu) (8)

as the basis of a statistical test. Higher values of tμt_{\mu} thus correspond to increasing incompatibility between the data and μ\mu.

We may define a test of a hypothesized value of μ\mu by using the statistic tμt_{\mu} directly as measure of discrepancy between the data and the hypothesis, with higher values of tμt_{\mu} correspond to increasing disagreement. To quantify the level of disagreement we compute the pp-value,

pμ=∫tμ,obs∞f⁡(tμ|μ)​d​tμ,p_{\mu}=\int_{t_{\mu,{\rm obs}}}^{\infty}f(t_{\mu}|\mu)\,dt_{\mu}\;, (9)

where tμ,obst_{\mu,{\rm obs}} is the value of the statistic tμt_{\mu} observed from the data and f⁡(tμ|μ)f(t_{\mu}|\mu) denotes the pdf of tμt_{\mu} under the assumption of the signal strength μ\mu. Useful approximations for this and other related pdfs are given in Sec. 3.3. The relation between the pp-value and the observed tμt_{\mu} and also with the significance ZZ are illustrated in Fig. 1.

When using the statistic tμt_{\mu}, a data set may result in a low pp-value in two distinct ways: the estimated signal strength μ^\hat{\mu} may be found greater or less than the hypothesized value μ\mu. As a result, the set of μ\mu values that are rejected because their pp-values are found below a specified threshold α\alpha may lie to either side of those values not rejected, i.e., one may obtain a two-sided confidence interval for μ\mu.

2.2 Test statistic t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu} for μ≥0\mu\geq 0

Often one assumes that the presence of a new signal can only increase the mean event rate beyond what is expected from background alone. That is, the signal process necessarily has μ≥0\mu\geq 0, and to take this into account we define an alternative test statistic below called t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu}.

For a model where μ≥0\mu\geq 0, if one finds data such that μ^<0\hat{\mu}<0, then the best level of agreement between the data and any physical value of μ\mu occurs for μ=0\mu=0. We therefore define

λ~​(μ)={L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L⁡(μ^,𝜽^)μ^≥0,L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L​(0,𝜽^^​(0))μ^<0.\tilde{\lambda}({\mu})=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}})}&\hat{\mu}\geq 0,\\[8.5359pt] \frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(0,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(0))}&\hat{\mu}<0\;.\end{array}\right. (10)

Here 𝜽^^​(0)\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(0) and 𝜽^^​(μ)\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu) refer to the conditional ML estimators of 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta given a strength parameter of 00 or μ\mu, respectively.

The variable λ~​(μ)\tilde{\lambda}(\mu) can be used instead of λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) in Eq. (8) to obtain the corresponding test statistic, which we denote t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu}. That is,

t~μ=−2​ln⁡λ~​(μ)={−2​ln⁡L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L​(0,θ^^​(0))μ^<0,−2​ln⁡L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L⁡(μ^,𝜽^)μ^≥0.\tilde{t}_{\mu}=-2\ln\tilde{\lambda}(\mu)=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}-2\ln\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(0,\hat{\hat{\theta}}(0))}&\quad\hat{\mu}<0\;,\\[5.69046pt] -2\ln\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}})}&\quad\hat{\mu}\geq 0\;.\end{array}\right. (11)

As was done with the statistic tμt_{\mu}, one can quantify the level of disagreement between the data and the hypothesized value of μ\mu with the pp-value, just as in Eq. (9). For this one needs the distribution of t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu}, an approximation of which is given in Sec. 3.4.

Also similar to the case of tμt_{\mu}, values of μ\mu both above and below μ^\hat{\mu} may be excluded by a given data set, i.e., one may obtain either a one-sided or two-sided confidence interval for μ\mu. For the case of no nuisance parameters, the test variable t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu} is equivalent to what is used in constructing confidence intervals according to the procedure of Feldman and Cousins [8].

2.3 Test statistic q0q_{0} for discovery of a positive signal

An important special case of the statistic t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu} described above is used to test μ=0\mu=0 in a class of model where we assume μ≥0\mu\geq 0. Rejecting the μ=0\mu=0 hypothesis effectively leads to the discovery of a new signal. For this important case we use the special notation q0=t~0q_{0}=\tilde{t}_{0}. Using the definition (11) with μ=0\mu=0 one finds

q0={−2​ln⁡λ​(0)μ^≥0,0μ^<0,q_{0}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}-2\ln\lambda(0)&\quad\hat{\mu}\geq 0\;,\\[8.5359pt] 0&\quad\hat{\mu}<0\;,\end{array}\right. (12)

where λ⁡(0)\lambda(0) is the profile likelihood ratio for μ=0\mu=0 as defined in Eq. (7).

We may contrast this to the statistic t0t_{0}, i.e., Eq. (8), used to test μ=0\mu=0. In that case one may reject the μ=0\mu=0 hypothesis for either an upward or downward fluctuation of the data. This is appropriate if the presence of a new phenomenon could lead to an increase or decrease in the number of events found. In an experiment looking for neutrino oscillations, for example, the signal hypothesis may predict a greater or lower event rate than the no-oscillation hypothesis.

When using q0q_{0}, however, we consider the data to show lack of agreement with the background-only hypothesis only if μ^>0\hat{\mu}>0. That is, a value of μ^\hat{\mu} much below zero may indeed constitute evidence against the background-only model, but this type of discrepancy does not show that the data contain signal events, but rather points to some other systematic error. For the present discussion, however, we assume that the systematic uncertainties are dealt with by the nuisance parameters 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta.

If the data fluctuate such that one finds fewer events than even predicted by background processes alone, then μ^<0\hat{\mu}<0 and one has q0=0q_{0}=0. As the event yield increases above the expected background, i.e., for increasing μ^\hat{\mu}, one finds increasingly large values of q0q_{0}, corresponding to an increasing level of incompatibility between the data and the μ=0\mu=0 hypothesis.

To quantify the level of disagreement between the data and the hypothesis of μ=0\mu=0 using the observed value of q0q_{0} we compute the pp-value in the same manner as done with tμt_{\mu}, namely,

p0=∫q0,obs∞f⁡(q0|0)​d​q0.p_{0}=\int_{q_{0,{\rm obs}}}^{\infty}f(q_{0}|0)\,dq_{0}\;. (13)

Here f⁡(q0|0)f(q_{0}|0) denotes the pdf of the statistic q0q_{0} under assumption of the background-only (μ=0\mu=0) hypothesis. An approximation for this and other related pdfs are given in Sec. 3.5.

2.4 Test statistic qμq_{\mu} for upper limits

For purposes of establishing an upper limit on the strength parameter μ\mu, we consider two closely related test statistics. First, we may define

qμ={−2​ln⁡λ​(μ)μ^≤μ,0μ^>μ,q_{\mu}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}-2\ln\lambda(\mu)&\hat{\mu}\leq\mu\;,\\[5.69046pt] 0&\hat{\mu}>\mu\;,\end{array}\right. (14)

where λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) is the profile likelihood ratio as defined in Eq. (7). The reason for setting qμ=0q_{\mu}=0 for μ^>μ\hat{\mu}>\mu is that when setting an upper limit, one would not regard data with μ^>μ\hat{\mu}>\mu as representing less compatibility with μ\mu than the data obtained, and therefore this is not taken as part of the rejection region of the test. From the definition of the test statistic one sees that higher values of qμq_{\mu} represent greater incompatibility between the data and the hypothesized value of μ\mu.

One should note that q0q_{0} is not simply a special case of qμq_{\mu} with μ=0\mu=0, but rather has a different definition (see Eqs. (12) and (14)). That is, q0q_{0} is zero if the data fluctuate downward (μ^<0\hat{\mu}<0), but qμq_{\mu} is zero if the data fluctuate upward (μ^>μ\hat{\mu}>\mu). With that caveat in mind, we will often refer in the following to qμq_{\mu} with the idea that this means either q0q_{0} or qμq_{\mu} as appropriate to the context.

As with the case of discovery, one quantifies the level of agreement between the data and hypothesized μ\mu with pp-value. For, e.g., an observed value qμ,obsq_{\mu,{\rm obs}}, one has

pμ=∫qμ,obs∞f⁡(qμ|μ)​d​qμ,p_{\mu}=\int_{q_{\mu,{\rm obs}}}^{\infty}f(q_{\mu}|\mu)\,dq_{\mu}\;, (15)

which can be expressed as a significance using Eq. (1). Here f⁡(qμ|μ)f(q_{\mu}|\mu) is the pdf of qμq_{\mu} assuming the hypothesis μ\mu. In Sec. 3.6 we provide useful approximations for this and other related pdfs.

2.5 Alternative test statistic q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} for upper limits

For the case where one considers models for which μ≥0\mu\geq 0, the variable λ~​(μ)\tilde{\lambda}(\mu) can be used instead of λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) in Eq. (14) to obtain the corresponding test statistic, which we denote q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}. That is,

q~μ={−2​ln⁡λ~​(μ)μ^≤μ0μ^>μ={−2​ln⁡L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L​(0,θ^^​(0))μ^<0,−2​ln⁡L​(μ,𝜽^^​(μ))L⁡(μ^,𝜽^)0≤μ^≤μ,0μ^>μ.\tilde{q}_{\mu}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}-2\ln\tilde{\lambda}(\mu)&\hat{\mu}\leq\mu\\[5.69046pt] 0&\hat{\mu}>\mu\end{array}\right.\quad=\quad\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{lll}-2\ln\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(0,\hat{\hat{\theta}}(0))}&\hat{\mu}<0\;,\\[5.69046pt] -2\ln\frac{L(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(\mu))}{L(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}})}&0\leq\hat{\mu}\leq\mu\;,\\[5.69046pt] 0&\hat{\mu}>\mu\;.\end{array}\right. (16)

We give an approximation for the pdf f⁡(q~μ|μ′)f(\tilde{q}_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) in Sec. 3.7.

In numerical examples we have found that the difference between the tests based on qμq_{\mu} (Eq. (14)) and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} usually to be negligible, but use of qμq_{\mu} leads to important simplifications. Furthermore, in the context of the approximation used in Sec. 3, the two statistics are equivalent. That is, assuming the approximations below, qμq_{\mu} can be expressed as a monotonic function of q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} and thus they lead to the same results.

3 Approximate sampling distributions

In order to find the pp-value of a hypothesis using Eqs. (13) or (15) we require the sampling distribution for the test statistic being used. In the case of discovery we are testing the background-only hypothesis (μ=0\mu=0) and therefore we need f⁡(q0|0)f(q_{0}|0), where q0q_{0} is defined by Eq. (12). When testing a nonzero value of μ\mu for purposes of finding an upper limit we need the distribution f⁡(qμ|μ)f(q_{\mu}|\mu) where qμq_{\mu} is defined by Eq. (14), or alternatively we require the pdf of the corresponding statistic q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} as defined by Eq. (16). In this notation the subscript of qq refers to the hypothesis being tested, and the second argument in f⁡(qμ|μ)f(q_{\mu}|\mu) gives the value of μ\mu assumed in the distribution of the data.

We also need the distribution f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) with μ≠μ′\mu\neq\mu^{\prime} to find what significance to expect and how this is distributed if the data correspond to a strength parameter different from the one being tested. For example, it is useful to characterize the sensitivity of a planned experiment by quoting the median significance, assuming data distributed according to a specified signal model, with which one would expect to exclude the background-only hypothesis. For this one would need f⁡(q0|μ′)f(q_{0}|\mu^{\prime}), usually with μ′=1\mu^{\prime}=1. From this one can find the median q0q_{0}, and thus the median discovery significance. When considering upper limits, one would usually quote the value of μ\mu for which the median pp-value is equal to 0.05, as this gives the median upper limit on μ\mu at 95% confidence level. In this case one would need f⁡(qμ|0)f(q_{\mu}|0) (or alternatively f⁡(q~μ|0)f(\tilde{q}_{\mu}|0)).

In Sec. 3.1 we present an approximation for the profile likelihood ratio, valid in the large sample limit. This allows one to obtain approximations for all of the required distributions, which are given in Sections 3.3 through 3.6 The approximations become exact in the large sample limit and are in fact found to provide accurate results even for fairly small sample sizes. For very small data samples one always has the possibility of using Monte Carlo methods to determine the required distributions.

3.1 Approximate distribution of the profile likelihood ratio

Consider a test of the strength parameter μ\mu, which here can either be zero (for discovery) or nonzero (for an upper limit), and suppose the data are distributed according to a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime}. The desired distribution f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) can be found using a result due to Wald [2], who showed that for the case of a single parameter of interest,

−2​ln⁡λ⁡(μ)=(μ−μ^)2σ2+𝒪⁡(1/N).-2\ln\lambda(\mu)=\frac{(\mu-\hat{\mu})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}+{\cal O}(1/\sqrt{N})\;. (17)

Here μ^\hat{\mu} follows a Gaussian distribution with a mean μ′\mu^{\prime} and standard deviation σ\sigma, and NN represents the data sample size. The standard deviation σ\sigma of μ^\hat{\mu} is obtained from the covariance matrix of the estimators for all the parameters, Vi​j=cov​[θ^i,θ^j]V_{ij}=\mbox{cov}[\hat{\theta}_{i},\hat{\theta}_{j}], where here the θi\theta_{i} represent both μ\mu as well as the nuisance parameters (e.g., take θ0=μ\theta_{0}=\mu, so σ2=V00\sigma^{2}=V_{00}). In the large-sample limit, the bias of ML estimators in general tend to zero, in which case we can write the inverse of the covariance matrix as

Vi​j−1=−E⁡[∂2ln⁡L∂θi​∂θj],V^{-1}_{ij}=-E\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ln L}{\partial\theta_{i}\partial\theta_{j}}\right]\;, (18)

where the expectation value assumes a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime}. The approximations presented here are valid to the extent that the 𝒪⁡(1/N){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{N}) term can be neglected, and the value of σ\sigma can be estimated, e.g., using Eq. (18). In Sec. 3.2 we present an alternative way to estimate σ\sigma which lends itself more directly to determination of the median significance.

If μ^\hat{\mu} is Gaussian distributed and we neglect the 𝒪⁡(1/N){\cal O}(1/\sqrt{N}) term in Eq. (17), then one can show that the statistic tμ=−2​ln⁡λ⁡(μ)t_{\mu}=-2\ln\lambda(\mu) follows a noncentral chi-square distribution for one degree of freedom (see, e.g., [9]),

f⁡(tμ,Λ)=12​tμ​12​π​[exp⁡(−12​(tμ+Λ)2)+exp⁡(−12​(tμ−Λ)2)],f(t_{\mu};\Lambda)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t_{\mu}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}+\sqrt{\Lambda}\right)^{2}\right)+\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}-\sqrt{\Lambda}\right)^{2}\right)\right]\;, (19)

where the noncentrality parameter Λ\Lambda is

Λ=(μ−μ′)2σ2.\Lambda=\frac{(\mu-\mu^{\prime})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\;. (20)

For the special case μ′=μ\mu^{\prime}=\mu one has Λ=0\Lambda=0 and −2​ln⁡λ​(μ)-2\ln\lambda(\mu) approaches a chi-square distribution for one degree of freedom, a result shown earlier by Wilks [1].

The results of Wilks and Wald generalize to more than one parameter of interest. If the parameters of interest can be explicitly identified with a subset of the parameters 𝜽r=(θ1,…,θrCLOSE\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{r}=(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{r}), then the distribution of −2​ln⁡λ⁡(𝜽r)-2\ln\lambda(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{r}) follows a noncentral chi-square distribution for rr-degrees of freedom with noncentrality parameter

Λr=∑i,j=1r(θi−θi′)​V~i​j−1​(θj−θj′),\Lambda_{r}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{r}(\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{\prime})\,\tilde{V}_{ij}^{-1}\,(\theta_{j}-\theta_{j}^{\prime})\;, (21)

where V~i​j−1\tilde{V}_{ij}^{-1} is the inverse of the submatrix one obtains from restricting the full covariance matrix to the parameters of interest. The full covariance matrix is given from inverting Eq. (18), and we show an efficient way to calculate it in Sec. 3.2.

3.2 The Asimov data set and the variance of μ^\hat{\mu}

Some of the formulae given require the standard deviation σ\sigma of μ^\hat{\mu}, which is assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution with a mean of μ′\mu^{\prime}. Below we show two ways of estimating σ\sigma, both of which are closely related to a special, artificial data set that we call the “Asimov data set”.

We define the Asimov data set such that when one uses it to evaluate the estimators for all parameters, one obtains the true parameter values. Consider the likelihood function for the generic analysis given by Eq. (6). To simplify the notation in this section we define

νi=μ′​si+bi.\nu_{i}=\mu^{\prime}s_{i}+b_{i}\;. (22)

Further let θ0=μ\theta_{0}=\mu represent the strength parameter, so that here θi\theta_{i} can stand for any of the parameters. The ML estimators for the parameters can be found by setting the derivatives of ln⁡L\ln L with respect to all of the parameters equal to zero:

∂ln⁡L∂θj=∑i=1N(niνi−1)​∂νi∂θj+∑i=1M(miui−1)​∂ui∂θj=0.\frac{\partial\ln L}{\partial\theta_{j}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{n_{i}}{\nu_{i}}-1\right)\frac{\partial\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}+\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left(\frac{m_{i}}{u_{i}}-1\right)\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}=0\;. (23)

This condition holds if the Asimov data, ni,An_{i,{\rm A}} and mi,Am_{i,{\rm A}}, are equal to their expectation values:

ni,A\displaystyle n_{i,{\rm A}} =\displaystyle= E⁡[ni]=νi=μ′​si​(𝜽)+bi​(𝜽),\displaystyle E[n_{i}]=\nu_{i}=\mu^{\prime}s_{i}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})+b_{i}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\;, (24)
mi,A\displaystyle m_{i,{\rm A}} =\displaystyle= E⁡[mi]=ui​(𝜽).\displaystyle E[m_{i}]=u_{i}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\;. (25)

Here the parameter values represent those implied by the assumed distribution of the data. In practice, these are the values that would be estimated from the Monte Carlo model using a very large data sample.

We can use the Asimov data set to evaluate the “Asimov likelihood” LAL_{\rm A} and the corresponding profile likelihood ratio λA\lambda_{\rm A}. The use of non-integer values for the data is not a problem as the factorial terms in the Poisson likelihood represent constants that cancel when forming the likelihood ratio, and thus can be dropped. One finds

λA​(μ)=LA​(μ,𝜽^^)LA​(μ^,𝜽^)=LA​(μ,𝜽^^)LA​(μ′,𝜽),\lambda_{\rm A}(\mu)=\frac{L_{\rm A}(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}})}{L_{\rm A}(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}})}=\frac{L_{\rm A}(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}})}{L_{A}(\mu^{\prime},\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})}\;, (26)

where the final equality above exploits the fact that the estimators for the parameters are equal to their hypothesized values when the likelihood is evaluated with the Asimov data set.

A standard way to find σ\sigma is by estimating the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood function (cf. Eq. (18)) to obtain the inverse covariance matrix V−1V^{-1}, inverting to find VV, and then extracting the element V00V_{00} corresponding to the variance of μ^\hat{\mu}. The second derivative of ln⁡L\ln L is

∂2ln⁡L∂θj​∂θk\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\ln L}{\partial\theta_{j}\partial\theta_{k}} =\displaystyle= ∑i=1N[(niνi−1)​∂2νi∂θj​∂θk−∂νi∂θj​∂νi∂θk​niνi2]\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\left(\frac{n_{i}}{\nu_{i}}-1\right)\frac{\partial^{2}\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}\partial\theta_{k}}-\frac{\partial\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}\frac{\partial\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\frac{n_{i}}{\nu_{i}^{2}}\right] (27)
+\displaystyle+ ∑i=1M[(miui−1)​∂2ui∂θj​∂θk−∂ui∂θj​∂ui∂θk​miui2].\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}\left[\left(\frac{m_{i}}{u_{i}}-1\right)\frac{\partial^{2}u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}\partial\theta_{k}}-\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\frac{m_{i}}{u_{i}^{2}}\right]\;.

From (27) one sees that the second derivative of ln⁡L\ln L is linear in the data values nin_{i} and mim_{i}. Thus its expectation value is found simply by evaluating with the expectation values of the data, which is the same as the Asimov data. One can therefore obtain the inverse covariance matrix from

Vj​k−1=−E⁡[∂2ln⁡L∂θj​∂θk]=−∂2ln⁡LA∂θj​∂θk=∑i=1N∂νi∂θj​∂νi∂θk​1νi+∑i=1M∂ui∂θj​∂ui∂θk​1ui.V^{-1}_{jk}=-E\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\ln L}{\partial\theta_{j}\partial\theta_{k}}\right]=-\frac{\partial^{2}\ln L_{\rm A}}{\partial\theta_{j}\partial\theta_{k}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\partial\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}\frac{\partial\nu_{i}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\frac{1}{\nu_{i}}+\sum_{i=1}^{M}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{j}}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\frac{1}{u_{i}}\;. (28)

In practice one could, for example, evaluate the the derivatives of ln⁡LA\ln L_{\rm A} numerically, use this to find the inverse covariance matrix, and then invert and extract the variance of μ^\hat{\mu}. One can see directly from Eq. (28) that this variance depends on the parameter values assumed for the Asimov data set, in particular on the assumed strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime}, which enters via Eq. (22).

Another method for estimating σ\sigma (denoted σA\sigma_{\rm A} in this section to distinguish it from the approach above based on the second derivatives of ln⁡L\ln L) is to find find the value that is necessary to recover the known properties of −λA​(μ)-\lambda_{\rm A}(\mu). Because the Asimov data set corresponding to a strength μ′\mu^{\prime} gives μ^=μ′\hat{\mu}=\mu^{\prime}, from Eq. (17) one finds

−2​ln⁡λA​(μ)≈(μ−μ′)2σ2=Λ.-2\ln\lambda_{\rm A}(\mu)\approx\frac{(\mu-\mu^{\prime})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}=\Lambda\;. (29)

That is, from the Asimov data set one obtains an estimate of the noncentrality parameter Λ\Lambda that characterizes the distribution f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}). Equivalently, one can use Eq. (29) to obtain the variance σ2\sigma^{2} which characterizes the distribution of μ^\hat{\mu}, namely,

σA2=(μ−μ′)2qμ,A,\sigma_{\rm A}^{2}=\frac{(\mu-\mu^{\prime})^{2}}{q_{\mu,{\rm A}}}\;, (30)

where qμ,A=−2​ln⁡λA​(μ)q_{\mu,{\rm A}}=-2\ln\lambda_{\rm A}(\mu). For the important case where one wants to find the median exclusion significance for the hypothesis μ\mu assuming that there is no signal, then one has μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0 and therefore

σA2=μ2qμ,A,\sigma_{\rm A}^{2}=\frac{\mu^{2}}{q_{\mu,{\rm A}}}\;, (31)

and for the modified statistic q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} the analogous relation holds. For the case of discovery where one tests μ=0\mu=0 one has

σA2=μ′ 2q0,A.\sigma_{\rm A}^{2}=\frac{\mu^{{\prime}\,2}}{q_{0,{\rm A}}}\;. (32)

The two methods for obtaining σ\sigma and Λ\Lambda — from the Fisher information matrix or from qμ,Aq_{\mu,\rm A} — are not identical, but were found to provide similar results in examples of of practical interest. In several cases that we considered, the distribution based on σA\sigma_{\rm A} provided a better approximation to the true sampling distribution than the standard approach based on the Fisher information matrix, leading to the conjecture that it may effectively incorporate some higher-order terms in Eq. (17).

This can be understood qualitatively by noting that under assumption of the Wald approximation, the test statistics q0q_{0}, qμq_{\mu} and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} are monotonically related to μ^\hat{\mu}, and therefore their median values can be found directly by using the median of μ^\hat{\mu}, which is μ′\mu^{\prime}. But monotonicity is a weaker condition than the full Wald approximation. That is, even if higher-order terms are present in Eq. (17), they will not alter the distribution’s median as long as they do not break the monotonicity of the relation between the test statistic and μ^\hat{\mu}. If one uses σA\sigma_{\rm A} one obtains distributions with medians given by the corresponding Asimov values, q0,Aq_{0,{\rm A}} or qμ,Aq_{\mu,{\rm A}}, and these values will be correct to the extent that monotonicity holds.

3.3 Distribution of tμt_{\mu}

Consider first using the statistic tμ=−2​ln⁡λ⁡(μ)t_{\mu}=-2\ln\lambda(\mu) of Sec. 2.1 as the basis of the statistical test of a hypothesized value of μ\mu. This could be a test of μ=0\mu=0 for purposes of establishing existence of a signal process, or non-zero values of μ\mu for purposes of obtaining a confidence interval. To find the pp-value pμp_{\mu}, we require the pdf f⁡(tμ|μ)f(t_{\mu}|\mu), and to find the median pp-value assuming a different strength parameter we will need f⁡(tμ|μ′)f(t_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}).

The pdf f⁡(tμ|μ′)f(t_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) is given by Eq. (19), namely,

f⁡(tμ|μ′)=12​tμ​12​π​[exp⁡(−12​(tμ+μ−μ′σ)2)+exp⁡(−12​(tμ−μ−μ′σ)2)].f(t_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t_{\mu}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}+\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right)+\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right)\right]\;. (33)

The special case μ=μ′\mu=\mu^{\prime} is simply a chi-square distribution for one degree of freedom:

f(tμ|μ)=12​π1tμe−tμ/2.f(t_{\mu}|\mu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{t_{\mu}}}e^{-t_{\mu}/2}\;. (34)

The cumulative distribution of tμt_{\mu} assuming μ′\mu^{\prime} is

F⁡(tμ|μ′)=Φ⁡(tμ+μ−μ′σ)+Φ⁡(tμ−μ−μ′σ)−1,F(t_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}+\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)+\Phi\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)-1\;, (35)

where Φ\Phi is the cumulative distribution of the standard (zero mean, unit variance) Gaussian. The special case μ=μ′\mu=\mu^{\prime} is therefore

F⁡(tμ|μ)=2​Φ​(tμ)−1,F(t_{\mu}|\mu)=2\Phi\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}\right)-1\;, (36)

The pp-value of a hypothesized value of μ\mu for an observed value tμt_{\mu} is therefore

pμ=1−F⁡(tμ|μ)=2​(1−Φ⁡(tμ)),p_{\mu}=1-F(t_{\mu}|\mu)=2\left(1-\Phi\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}\right)\right)\;, (37)

and the corresponding significance is

Zμ=Φ−1​(1−pμ)=Φ−1​(2​Φ​(tμ)−1).Z_{\mu}=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_{\mu})=\Phi^{-1}\left(2\Phi\left(\sqrt{t_{\mu}}\right)-1\right)\;. (38)

If the pp-value is found below a specified threshold α\alpha (often one takes α=0.05\alpha=0.05), then the value of μ\mu is said to be excluded at a confidence level (CL) of 1−α1-\alpha. The set of points not excluded form a confidence interval with CL=1−α\mbox{CL}=1-\alpha. Here the endpoints of the interval can be obtained simply by setting pμ=αp_{\mu}=\alpha and solving for μ\mu. Assuming the Wald approximation (17) and using Eq. (37) one finds

μup/lo=μ^±σ​Φ−1​(1−α/2).\mu_{\rm up/lo}=\hat{\mu}\pm\sigma\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\;. (39)

One subtlety with this formula is that σ\sigma itself depends at some level on μ\mu. In practice to find the upper and lower limits one can simply solve numerically to find those values of μ\mu that satisfy pμ=αp_{\mu}=\alpha.

3.4 Distribution of t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu}

Assuming the Wald approximation, the statistic t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu} as defined by Eq. (11) can be written

t~μ={μ2σ2−2​μ​μ^σ2μ^<0,(μ−μ^)2σ2μ^≥0.\tilde{t}_{\mu}=\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{\mu^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\frac{2\mu\hat{\mu}}{\sigma^{2}}&\quad\hat{\mu}<0\;,\\[5.69046pt] \frac{(\mu-\hat{\mu})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}&\quad\hat{\mu}\geq 0\;.\end{array}\right. (40)

From this the pdf f⁡(t~μ|μ′)f(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) is found to be

f⁡(t~μ|μ′)\displaystyle f(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= 12​12​π​1t~μ​exp⁡[−12​(t~μ+μ−μ′σ)2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}}\exp\left[-\mbox{\small$\frac{1}{2}$}\left(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}+\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right] (41)
+\displaystyle+ {12​12​π​1t~μ​exp⁡[−12​(t~μ−μ−μ′σ)2]t~μ≤μ2/σ2,12​π​(2​μ/σ)​exp⁡[−12​(t~μ−μ2−2​μ​μ′σ2)2(2​μ/σ)2]t~μ>μ2/σ2.\displaystyle\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}}\exp\left[-\mbox{\small$\frac{1}{2}$}\left(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right]&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}\leq\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;,\\[14.22636pt] \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}(2\mu/\sigma)}\exp\left[-\mbox{\small$\frac{1}{2}$}\frac{\left(\tilde{t}_{\mu}-\frac{\mu^{2}-2\mu\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}}{(2\mu/\sigma)^{2}}\right]&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}>\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\end{array}\right.\;.

The special case μ=μ′\mu=\mu^{\prime} is therefore

f⁡(t~μ|μ′)={12​π1t~μe−t~μ/2t~μ≤μ2/σ2,1212​π1t~μe−t~μ/2+12​π​(2​μ/σ)exp[−12(t~μ+μ2/σ2)2(2​μ/σ)2]t~μ>μ2/σ2..f(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}}e^{-\tilde{t}_{\mu}/2}&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}\leq\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;,\\[14.22636pt] \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}}e^{-\tilde{t}_{\mu}/2}\>+\>\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}(2\mu/\sigma)}\exp\left[-\mbox{\small$\frac{1}{2}$}\frac{(\tilde{t}_{\mu}+\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2})^{2}}{(2\mu/\sigma)^{2}}\right]&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}>\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;.\end{array}\right.\;. (45)

The corresponding cumulative distribution is

F⁡(t~μ|μ′)=Φ⁡(t~μ+μ−μ′σ)+{Φ⁡(t~μ−μ−μ′σ)−1t~μ≤μ2/σ2,Φ⁡(t~μ−(μ2−2​μ​μ′)/σ22​μ/σ)−1t~μ>μ2/σ2.F(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}+\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)+\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\Phi\left(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)-1&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}\leq\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;,\\[14.22636pt] \Phi\left(\frac{\tilde{t}_{\mu}-(\mu^{2}-2\mu\mu^{\prime})/\sigma^{2}}{2\mu/\sigma}\right)-1&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}>\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;.\end{array}\right. (46)

For μ=μ′\mu=\mu^{\prime} this is

F⁡(t~μ|μ)={2​Φ​(t~μ)−1t~μ≤μ2/σ2,Φ⁡(t~μ)+Φ⁡(t~μ+μ2/σ22​μ/σ)−1t~μ>μ2/σ2.F(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu)=\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}2\Phi\Big(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}\Big)-1&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}\leq\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;,\\[14.22636pt] \Phi\Big(\sqrt{\tilde{t}_{\mu}}\Big)+\Phi\left(\frac{\tilde{t}_{\mu}+\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}}{2\mu/\sigma}\right)-1&\quad\tilde{t}_{\mu}>\mu^{2}/\sigma^{2}\;.\end{array}\right. pμ=1−F⁡(t~μ|μ).p_{\mu}=1-F(\tilde{t}_{\mu}|\mu)\;. (48)

The corresponding significance is Zμ=Φ−1​(1−pμ)Z_{\mu}=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_{\mu}).

A confidence interval for μ\mu at confidence level CL=1−α\mbox{CL}=1-\alpha can be constructed from the set μ\mu values for which the pp-value is not less than α\alpha. To find the endpoints of this interval, one can set pμp_{\mu} from Eq. (48) equal to α\alpha and solve for μ\mu. In general this must be done numerically. In the large sample limit, i.e., assuming the validity of the asymptotic approximations, these intervals correspond to the limits of Feldman and Cousins [8] for the case where physical range of the parameter μ\mu is μ≥0\mu\geq 0.

3.5 Distribution of q0q_{0} (discovery)

Assuming the validity of the approximation (17), one has −2​ln⁡λ⁡(0)=μ^2/σ2-2\ln\lambda(0)=\hat{\mu}^{2}/\sigma^{2}. From the definition (12) of q0q_{0}, we therefore have

q0={μ^2/σ2μ^≥0,0μ^<0,q_{0}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\hat{\mu}^{2}/\sigma^{2}&\quad\hat{\mu}\geq 0\;,\\[8.5359pt] 0&\quad\hat{\mu}<0\;,\end{array}\right. (49)

where μ^\hat{\mu} follows a Gaussian distribution with mean μ′\mu^{\prime} and standard deviation σ\sigma. From this one can show that the pdf of q0q_{0} has the form

f⁡(q0|μ′)=(1−Φ⁡(μ′σ))​δ​(q0)+12​12​π​1q0​exp⁡[−12​(q0−μ′σ)2].f(q_{0}|\mu^{\prime})=\left(1-\Phi\left(\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)\right)\delta(q_{0})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{0}}}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{q_{0}}-\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right]\;. (50)

For the special case of μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0, this reduces to

f(q0|0)=12δ(q0)+1212​π1q0e−q0/2.f(q_{0}|0)=\frac{1}{2}\delta(q_{0})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{0}}}e^{-q_{0}/2}\;. (51)

That is, one finds a mixture of a delta function at zero and a chi-square distribution for one degree of freedom, with each term having a weight of 1/21/2. In the following we will refer to this mixture as a half chi-square distribution or 12​χ12\mbox{\small$\frac{1}{2}$}\chi^{2}_{1}.

From Eq. (50) the corresponding cumulative distribution is found to be

F⁡(q0|μ′)=Φ⁡(q0−μ′σ).F(q_{0}|\mu^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\sqrt{q_{0}}-\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)\;. (52)

The important special case μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0 is therefore simply

F⁡(q0|0)=Φ⁡(q0).F(q_{0}|0)=\Phi\Big(\sqrt{q_{0}}\Big)\;. (53)

The pp-value of the μ=0\mu=0 hypothesis (see Eq. (13)) is

p0=1−F⁡(q0|0),p_{0}=1-F(q_{0}|0)\;, (54)

and therefore using Eq. (1) for the significance one obtains the simple formula

Z0=Φ−1​(1−p0)=q0.Z_{0}=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_{0})=\sqrt{q_{0}}\;. (55)

3.6 Distribution of qμq_{\mu} (upper limits)

Assuming the validity of the Wald approximation, we can write the test statistic used for upper limits, Eq. (14) as

qμ={(μ−μ^)2σ2μ^<μ,0μ^>μ,q_{\mu}=\quad\>\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{lll}\frac{(\mu-\hat{\mu})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}&\hat{\mu}<\mu\;,\\[5.69046pt] 0&\hat{\mu}>\mu\;,\end{array}\right. (56)

where μ^\hat{\mu} as before follows a Gaussian centred about μ′\mu^{\prime} with a standard deviation σ\sigma.

The pdf f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) is found to be

f⁡(qμ|μ′)=Φ⁡(μ′−μσ)​δ​(qμ)+12​12​π​1qμ​exp⁡[−12​(qμ−μ−μ′σ)2],f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\frac{\mu^{\prime}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\delta(q_{\mu})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{\mu}}}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{q_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right]\;, (57)

so that the special case μ=μ′\mu=\mu^{\prime} is a half-chi-square distribution:

f(qμ|μ)=12δ(qμ)+1212​π1qμe−qμ/2.f(q_{\mu}|\mu)=\frac{1}{2}\delta(q_{\mu})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{q_{\mu}}}e^{-q_{\mu}/2}\;. (58)

The cumulative distribution is

F⁡(qμ|μ′)=Φ⁡(qμ−μ−μ′σ),F(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime})=\Phi\left(\sqrt{q_{\mu}}-\frac{\mu-\mu^{\prime}}{\sigma}\right)\;, (59)

and the corresponding special case μ′=μ\mu^{\prime}=\mu is thus the same as what was found for q0q_{0}, namely,

F⁡(qμ|μ)=Φ⁡(qμ).F(q_{\mu}|\mu)=\Phi\Big(\sqrt{q_{\mu}}\Big)\;. (60)

The pp-value of the hypothesized μ\mu is

pμ=1−F⁡(qμ|μ)=1−Φ⁡(qμ)p_{\mu}=1-F(q_{\mu}|\mu)=1-\Phi\Big(\sqrt{q_{\mu}}\Big) (61)

and therefore the corresponding significance is

Zμ=Φ−1​(1−pμ)=qμ.Z_{\mu}=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_{\mu})=\sqrt{q_{\mu}}\;. (62)

As with the statistic tμt_{\mu} above, if the pp-value is found below a specified threshold α\alpha (often one takes α=0.05\alpha=0.05), then the value of μ\mu is said to be excluded at a confidence level (CL) of 1−α1-\alpha. The upper limit on μ\mu is the largest μ\mu with pμ≤αp_{\mu}\leq\alpha. Here this can be obtained simply by setting pμ=αp_{\mu}=\alpha and solving for μ\mu. Using Eqs. (56) and (61) one finds

μup=μ^+σ​Φ−1​(1−α).\mu_{\rm up}=\hat{\mu}+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\;. (63)

For example, α=0.05\alpha=0.05 gives Φ−1​(1−α)=1.64\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)=1.64. Also as noted above, σ\sigma depends in general on the hypothesized μ\mu. Thus in practice one may find the upper limit numerically as the value of μ\mu for which pμ=αp_{\mu}=\alpha.
