3.8 Distribution of −2​ln⁡(Ls+b/Lb)-2\ln(L_{s+b}/L_{b})

Many analyses carried out at the Tevatron Collider (e.g., [10]) involving searches for a new signal process have been based on the statistic

q=−2​ln⁡Ls+bLb,q=-2\ln\frac{L_{s+b}}{L_{b}}\;, (74)

where Ls+bL_{s+b} is the likelihood of the nominal signal model and LbL_{b} is that of the background-only hypothesis. That is, the s+bs+b corresponds to having the strength parameter μ=1\mu=1 and LbL_{b} refers to μ=0\mu=0. The statistic qq can therefore be written

q=−2​ln⁡L​(μ=1,𝜽^^​(1))L​(μ=0,𝜽^^​(0))=−2​ln⁡λ⁡(1)+2​ln⁡λ⁡(0).q=-2\ln\frac{L(\mu=1,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(1))}{L(\mu=0,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}(0))}=-2\ln\lambda(1)+2\ln\lambda(0)\;. (75)

Assuming the validity of the Wald approximation (17), qq is given by

q=(μ^−1)2σ2−μ^2σ2=1−2​μ^σ2,q=\frac{(\hat{\mu}-1)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}-\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}=\frac{1-2\hat{\mu}}{\sigma^{2}}\;, (76)

where as previously σ2\sigma^{2} is the variance of μ^\hat{\mu}. As μ^\hat{\mu} follows a Gaussian distribution, the distribution of qq is also seen to be Gaussian, with a mean value of

E⁡[q]=1−2​μσ2E[q]=\frac{1-2\mu}{\sigma^{2}} (77)

and a variance of

V⁡[q]=4σ2.V[q]=\frac{4}{\sigma^{2}}\;. (78)

That is, the standard deviation of qq is σq=2/σ\sigma_{q}=2/\sigma, where the standard deviation of μ^\hat{\mu}, σ\sigma, can be estimated, e.g., using the second derivatives of the log-likelihood function as described in Sec. 3.1 or with the methods discussed in Sec. 3.2. Recall that in general σ\sigma depends on the hypothesized value of μ\mu; here we will refer to these as σb\sigma_{b} and σs+b\sigma_{s+b} for the μ=0\mu=0 and μ=1\mu=1 hypotheses, respectively.

From Eq. (77) one sees that for the s+bs+b hypothesis (μ=1\mu=1) the values of qq tend to be lower, and for the bb hypothesis (μ=0\mu=0) they are higher. Therefore we can find the pp-values for the two hypothesis from

ps+b\displaystyle p_{s+b} =\displaystyle= ∫qobs∞f⁡(q|s+b)​𝑑q=1−Φ⁡(qobs+1/σs+b22/σs+b),\displaystyle\int_{q_{\rm obs}}^{\infty}f(q|s+b)\,dq=1-\Phi\left(\frac{q_{\rm obs}+1/\sigma_{s+b}^{2}}{2/\sigma_{s+b}}\right)\;, (79)
pb\displaystyle p_{b} =\displaystyle= ∫−∞qobsf⁡(q|b)​𝑑q=Φ⁡(qobs−1/σb22/σb),\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{q_{\rm obs}}f(q|b)\,dq=\Phi\left(\frac{q_{\rm obs}-1/\sigma_{b}^{2}}{2/\sigma_{b}}\right)\;, (80)

where we have used Eqs. (77) and (78) for the mean and variance of qq under the bb and s+bs+b hypotheses.

The pp-values from Eqs. (79) and (80) incorporate the effects of systematic uncertainties to the extent that these are connected to the nuisance parameters 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta. In analyses done at the Tevatron such as in Ref. [10], these effects are incorporated into the distribution of qq in a different but largely equivalent way. There, usually one treats the control measurements that constrain the nuisance parameters as fixed, and to determine the distribution of qq one only generates the main search measurement (i.e., what corresponds in our generic analysis to the histogram 𝐧\textstyle\bf n). The effects of the systematic uncertainties are taken into account by using the control measurements as the basis of a Bayesian prior density π⁡(𝜽)\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}), and the distribution of qq is computed under assumption of the Bayesian model average

f⁡(q)=∫f⁡(q|𝜽)​π​(𝜽)​𝑑𝜽.f(q)=\int f(q|\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\,d\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}\;. (81)

The prior pdf π⁡(𝜽)\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}) used in Eq. (81) would be obtained from some measurements characterized by a likelihood function L𝜽​(𝜽)L_{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}), and then used to find the prior π⁡(𝜽)\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}) using Bayes’ theorem,

π⁡(𝜽)∝L𝜽​(𝜽)​π0​(𝜽).\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\propto L_{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\pi_{0}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})\;. (82)

Here π0​(𝜽)\pi_{0}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}) is the initial prior for 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta that reflected one’s knowledge before carrying out the control measurements. In many cases this is simply take as a constant, in which case π⁡(𝜽)\pi(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}) is simply proportional to L𝜽​(𝜽)L_{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}).

In the approach of this paper, however, all measurements are regarded as part of the data, including control measurements that constrain nuisance parameters. That is, here to generate a data set by MC means, for a given assumed point in the model’s parameter space, one simulates both the control measurements and the main measurement. Although this is done for a specific value of 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta, in the asymptotic limit the distributions required for computing the pp-values (79) and (80) are only weakly dependent on 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta to the extent that this can affect the standard deviation σq\sigma_{q}. By contrast, in the Tevatron approach one generates only the main measurement with data distributed according to the averaged model (81). In the case where the nuisance parameters are constrained by Gaussian distributed estimates and the initial prior π0​(𝜽)\pi_{0}(\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}) is taken to be constant, the two methods are essentially equivalent.

Assuming the Wald approximation holds, the statistic qq as well as q0q_{0} from Eq. (12), qμq_{\mu} from Eq. (14) and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} from Eq. (16) are all monotonic functions of μ^\hat{\mu}, and therefore all are equivalent to μ^\hat{\mu} in terms of yielding the same statistical test. If there are no nuisance parameters, then the Neyman–Pearson lemma (see, e.g., [7]) states that the likelihood ratio Ls+b/LbL_{s+b}/L_{b} (or equivalently qq) is an optimal test statistic in the sense that it gives the maximum power for a test of the background-only hypothesis with respect to the alternative of signal plus background (and vice versa). But if the Wald approximation holds, then q0q_{0} and qμq_{\mu} lead to equivalent tests and are therefore also optimal in the Neyman–Pearson sense. If the nuisance parameters are well constrained by control measurements, then one expects this equivalence to remain approximately true.

Finally, note that in many analyses carried out at the Tevatron, hypothesized signal models are excluded based not on whether the pp-value ps+bp_{s+b} from Eq. (79) is less than a given threshold α\alpha, but rather the ratio CLs=ps+b/(1−pb)\mbox{CL}_{s}=p_{s+b}/(1-p_{b}) is compared to α\alpha. We do not consider this final step here; it is discussed in, e.g., Ref. [12].

4 Experimental sensitivity

To characterize the sensitivity of an experiment, one is interested not in the significance obtained from a single data set, but rather in the expected (more precisely, median) significance with which one would be able to reject different values of μ\mu. Specifically, for the case of discovery one would like to know the median, under the assumption of the nominal signal model (μ=1\mu=1), with which one would reject the background-only (μ=0\mu=0) hypothesis. And for the case of setting exclusion limits the sensitivity is characterized by the median significance, assuming data generated using the μ=0\mu=0 hypothesis, with which one rejects a nonzero value of μ\mu (usually μ=1\mu=1 is of greatest interest).

The sensitivity of an experiment is illustrated in Fig. 2, which shows the pdf for qμq_{\mu} assuming both a strength parameter μ\mu and also assuming a different value μ′\mu^{\prime}. The distribution f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) is shifted to higher value of qμq_{\mu}, corresponding on average to lower pp-values. The sensitivity of an experiment can be characterized by giving the pp-value corresponding to the median qμq_{\mu} assuming the alternative value μ′\mu^{\prime}. As the pp-value is a monotonic function of qμq_{\mu}, this is equal to the median pp-value assuming μ′\mu^{\prime}.

In the rest of this section we describe the ingredients needed to determine the experimental sensitivity (median discovery or exclusion significance). In Sec. 3.2 we introduced the Asimov data set, in which all statistical fluctuations are suppressed. This will lead directly to estimates of the experimental sensitivity (Sec. 4.1) as well as providing an alternative estimate of the standard deviation σ\sigma of the estimator μ^\hat{\mu}. In Sec. 4.2 we indicate how the procedure can be extended to the case where several search channels are combined, and in Sec. 4.3 we describe how to give statistical error bands for the sensitivity.

4.1 The median significance from Asimov values of the test statistic

By using the Asimov data set one can easily obtain the median values of q0q_{0}, qμq_{\mu} and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}, and these lead to simple expressions for the corresponding median significance. From Eqs. (55), (62) and (72) one sees that the significance ZZ is a monotonic function of qq, and therefore the median ZZ is simply given by the corresponding function of the median of qq, which is approximated by its Asimov value. For discovery using q0q_{0} one wants the median discovery significance assuming a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime} and for upper limits one is particularly interested in the median exclusion significance assuming μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0, med​[Zμ|0]\mbox{med}[Z_{\mu}|0]. For these one obtains

med​[Z0|μ′]\displaystyle\mbox{med}[Z_{0}|\mu^{\prime}] =\displaystyle= q0,A,\displaystyle\sqrt{q_{0,{\rm A}}}\;, (83)
med​[Zμ|0]\displaystyle\mbox{med}[Z_{\mu}|0] =\displaystyle= qμ,A.\displaystyle\sqrt{q_{\mu,{\rm A}}}\;. (84)

When using q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} for establishing upper limits, the general expression for the exclusion significance ZμZ_{\mu} is somewhat more complicated depending on μ′\mu^{\prime}, but is in any case found by substituting the appropriate values of q~μ,A\tilde{q}_{\mu,{\rm A}} and σA\sigma_{\rm A} into Eq. (72). For the usual case where one wants the median significance for μ\mu assuming data distributed according to the background-only hypothesis (μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0), Eq. (72) reduces in fact to a relation of the same form as Eq. (62), and therefore one finds

med​[Zμ|0]=q~μ,A.\mbox{med}[Z_{\mu}|0]=\sqrt{\tilde{q}_{\mu,{\rm A}}}\;. (85)

4.2 Combining multiple channels

In many analyses, there can be several search channels which need to be combined. For each channel ii there is a likelihood function Li​(μ,𝜽i)L_{i}(\mu,\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{i}), where 𝜽i\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{i} represents the set of nuisance parameters for the iith channel, some of which may be common between channels. Here the strength parameter μ\mu is assumed to be the same for all channels. If the channels are statistically independent, as can usually be arranged, the full likelihood function is given by the product over all of the channels,

L⁡(μ,𝜽)=∏iLi​(μ,𝜽i),L(\mu,\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})=\prod_{i}L_{i}(\mu,\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{i})\;, (86)

where 𝜽\textstyle\bf\theta represents the complete set of all nuisance parameters. The profile likelihood ratio λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) is therefore

λ⁡(μ)=∏iLi​(μ,𝜽^^i)∏iLi​(μ^,𝜽^i).\lambda(\mu)=\frac{\prod_{i}L_{i}(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}_{i})}{\prod_{i}L_{i}(\hat{\mu},\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}_{i})}\;. (87)

Because the Asimov data contain no statistical fluctuations, one has μ^=μ′\hat{\mu}=\mu^{\prime} for all channels. Furthermore any common components of 𝜽i\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}_{i} are the same for all channels. Therefore when using the Asimov data corresponding to a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime} one finds

λA​(μ)=∏iLi​(μ,𝜽^^)∏iLi​(μ′,𝜽)=∏iλA,i​(μ),\lambda_{\rm A}(\mu)=\frac{\prod_{i}L_{i}(\mu,\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}})}{\prod_{i}L_{i}(\mu^{\prime},\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}})}=\prod_{i}\lambda_{{\rm A},i}(\mu)\;, (88)

where λA,i​(μ)\lambda_{{\rm A},i}(\mu) is the profile likelihood ratio for the iith channel alone.

Because of this, it is possible to determine the values of the profile likelihood ratio entering into (88) separately for each channel, which simplifies greatly the task of estimating the median significance that would result from the full combination. It should be emphasized, however, that to find the discovery significance or exclusion limits determined from real data, one needs to construct the full likelihood function containing a single parameter μ\mu, and this must be used in a global fit to find the profile likelihood ratio.

4.3 Expected statistical variation (error bands)

By using the Asimov data set we can find the median, assuming some strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime} of the significance for rejecting a hypothesized value μ\mu. Even if the hypothesized value μ′\mu^{\prime} is correct, the actual data will contain statistical fluctuations and thus the observed significance is not in general equal to the median.

For example, if the signal is in fact absent but the number of background events fluctuates upward, then the observed upper limit on the parameter μ\mu will be weaker than the median assuming background only. It is useful to know by how much the significance is expected to vary, given the expected fluctuations in the data. As we have formulae for all of the relevant sampling distributions, we can also predict how the significance is expected to vary under assumption of a given signal strength.

It is convenient to calculate error bands for the median significance corresponding to the ±N​σ\pm N\sigma variation of μ^\hat{\mu}. As μ^\hat{\mu} is Gaussian distributed, these error bands on the significance are simply the quantiles that map onto the variation of μ^\hat{\mu} of ±N​σ\pm N\sigma about μ′\mu^{\prime}.

For the case of discovery, i.e., a test of μ=0\mu=0, one has from Eqs. (49) and (55) that the significance Z0Z_{0} is

Z0={μ^/σμ^≥0,0μ^<0.Z_{0}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\hat{\mu}/\sigma&\quad\hat{\mu}\geq 0\;,\\[8.5359pt] 0&\quad\hat{\mu}<0\;.\end{array}\right. (89)

Furthermore the median significance is found from Eq. (83), so the significance values corresponding to μ′±N​σ\mu^{\prime}\pm N\sigma are therefore

Z0​(μ′+N​σ)\displaystyle Z_{0}(\mu^{\prime}+N\sigma) =\displaystyle= med​[Z|μ′]+N,\displaystyle\mbox{med}[Z|\mu^{\prime}]+N\;, (90)
Z0​(μ′−N​σ)\displaystyle Z_{0}(\mu^{\prime}-N\sigma) =\displaystyle= max​[med​[Z|μ′]−N,0].\displaystyle\mbox{max}\left[\mbox{med}[Z|\mu^{\prime}]-N,0\right]\;. (91)

For the case of exclusion, when using both the statistic qμq_{\mu} as well as q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} one found the same expression for the upper limit at a confidence level of 1−α1-\alpha, namely, Eq. (63). Therefore the median upper limit assuming a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime} is found simply by substituting this for μ^\hat{\mu}, and the ±N​σ\pm N\sigma error bands are found similarly by substituting the corresponding values of μ′±N​σ\mu^{\prime}\pm N\sigma. That is, the median upper limit is

med​[μup|μ′]=μ′+σ​Φ−1​(1−α),\mbox{med}[\mu_{\rm up}|\mu^{\prime}]=\mu^{\prime}+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\;, (92)

and the ±N​σ\pm N\sigma error band is given by

bandN​σ=μ′+σ⁡(Φ−1​(1−α)±N).\mbox{band}_{N\sigma}=\mu^{\prime}+\sigma(\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\pm N)\;. (93)

The standard deviation σ\sigma of μ^\hat{\mu} can be obtained from the Asimov value of the test statistic qμq_{\mu} (or q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}) using Eq. (30).

5 Examples

In this section we describe two examples, both of which are special cases of the generic analysis described in Section 2. Here one has a histogram 𝐧=(n1,…,nN)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf n$}}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{N}) for the main measurement where signal events could be present and one may have another histogram 𝐦=(m1,…,mM)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf m$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf m$}}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{M}) as a control measurement, which helps constrain the nuisance parameters. In Section 5.1 we treat the simple case where each of these two measurements consists of a single Poisson distributed value, i.e., the histograms each have a single bin. We refer to this as a “counting experiment”. In Section 5.2 we consider multiple bins for the main histogram, but without a control histogram; here the measured shape of the main histogram on either side of the signal peak is sufficient to constrain the background. We refer to this as a “shape analysis”.

5.1 Counting experiment

Consider an experiment where one observes a number of events nn, assumed to follow a Poisson distribution with an expectation value E⁡[n]=μ​s+bE[n]=\mu s+b. Here ss represents the mean number of events from a signal model, which we take to be a known value; bb is the expected number from background processes, and as usual μ\mu is the strength parameter.

We will treat bb as a nuisance parameter whose value is constrained by a control measurement. This measurement is also a single Poisson distributed value mm with mean value E⁡[m]=τ​bE[m]=\tau b. That is, τ​b\tau b plays the role of the function uu for the single bin of the control histogram in Eq. (5). In a real analysis, the value of the scale factor τ\tau may have some uncertainty and could be itself treated as a nuisance parameter, but in this example we will take its value to be known. Related aspects of this type of analysis have been discussed in the literature, where it is sometimes referred to as the “on-off problem” (see, e.g., [11, 13]).

The data thus consist of two measured values: nn and mm. We have one parameter of interest, μ\mu, and one nuisance parameter, bb. The likelihood function for μ\mu and bb is the product of two Poisson terms:

L⁡(μ,b)=(μ​s+b)nn!​e−(μ​s+b)​(τ​b)mm!​e−τ​b.L(\mu,b)=\frac{(\mu s+b)^{n}}{n!}e^{-(\mu s+b)}\,\frac{(\tau b)^{m}}{m!}e^{-\tau b}\;. (94)

To find the test statistics q0q_{0}, qμq_{\mu} and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}, we require the ML estimators μ^\hat{\mu}, b^\hat{b} as well as the conditional ML estimator b^^\hat{\hat{b}} for a specified μ\mu. These are found to be

μ^\displaystyle\hat{\mu} =\displaystyle= n−m/τs,\displaystyle\frac{n-m/\tau}{s}\;, (95)
b^\displaystyle\hat{b} =\displaystyle= mτ,\displaystyle\frac{m}{\tau}\;, (96)
b^^\displaystyle\hat{\hat{b}} =\displaystyle= n+m−(1+τ)​μ​s2​(1+τ)+[(n+m−(1+τ)​μ​s)2+4​(1+τ)​m​μ​s4​(1+τ)2]1/2.\displaystyle\frac{n+m-(1+\tau)\mu s}{2(1+\tau)}+\left[\frac{(n+m-(1+\tau)\mu s)^{2}+4(1+\tau)m\mu s}{4(1+\tau)^{2}}\right]^{1/2}\;. (97)

Given measured values nn and mm, the estimators from Eqs. (95), (96) and (97) can be used in the likelihood function (94) to find the values of the test statistics q0q_{0}, qμq_{\mu} and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}. By generating data values nn and mm by Monte Carlo we can compare the resulting distributions with the formulae from Section 3.

The pdf f⁡(q0|0)f(q_{0}|0), i.e., the distribution of q0q_{0} for under the assumption of μ=0\mu=0, is shown in Fig. 3(a). The histograms show the result from Monte Carlo simulation based on several different values of the mean background bb. The solid curve shows the prediction of Eq. (51), which is independent of the nuisance parameter bb. The point at which one finds a significant departure between the histogram and the asymptotic formula occurs at increasingly large q0q_{0} for increasing bb. For b=20b=20 the agreement is already quite accurate past q0=25q_{0}=25, corresponding to a significance of Z=q0=5Z=\sqrt{q_{0}}=5. Even for b=2b=2 there is good agreement out to q0≈10q_{0}\approx 10.

Figure 3(b) shows distributions of q0q_{0} assuming a strength parameter μ′\mu^{\prime} equal to 0 and 1. The histograms show the Monte Carlo simulation of the corresponding distributions using the parameters s=10s=10, b=10b=10, τ=1\tau=1. For the distribution f⁡(q0|1)f(q_{0}|1) from Eq. (50), one requires the value of σ\sigma, the standard deviation of μ^\hat{\mu} assuming a strength parameter μ′=1\mu^{\prime}=1. Here this was determined from Eq. (32) using the Asimov value q0,Aq_{0,{\rm A}}, i.e., the value obtained from the Asimov data set with n→μ′​s+bn\rightarrow\mu^{\prime}s+b and m→τ​bm\rightarrow\tau b.

We can investigate the accuracy of the approximations used by comparing the discovery significance for a given observed value of q0q_{0} from the approximate formula with the exact significance determined using a Monte Carlo calculation. Figure 4(a) shows the discovery significance that one finds from q0=16q_{0}=16. According to Eq. (55), this should give a nominal significance of Z=q0=4Z=\sqrt{q_{0}}=4, indicated in the figure by the horizontal line. The points show the exact significance for different values of the expected number of background events bb in the counting analysis with a scale factor τ=1\tau=1. As can be seen, the approximation underestimates the significance for very low bb, but achieves an accuracy of better than 10% for bb greater than around 4. It slightly overestimates for bb greater than around 5. This phenomenon can be seen in the tail of f⁡(q0|0)f(q_{0}|0) in Fig. 3(b), which uses b=10b=10. The accuracy then rapidly improves for increasing bb.

Figure 4(b) shows the median value of the statistic q0q_{0} assuming data distributed according to the nominal signal hypothesis from Monte Carlo (points) and the value based on the Asimov data set as a function of bb for different values of ss, using a scale factor τ=1\tau=1. One can see that the Asimov data set leads to an excellent approximation to the median, except at very low ss and bb.

Figure 5(a) shows the distribution of the test statistic q1q_{1} for s=6s=6, b=9b=9, τ=1\tau=1 for data corresponding to a strength parameter μ′=1\mu^{\prime}=1 and also μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0. The vertical lines indicate the Asimov values of q1q_{1} and q~1\tilde{q}_{1} assuming a strength parameter μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0. These lines correspond to estimates of the median values of the test statistics assuming μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0. The areas under the curves f⁡(q1|1)f(q_{1}|1) and f⁡(q~1|1)f(\tilde{q}_{1}|1) to the right of this line give the median pp-values.

For the example described above we can also find the distribution of the statistic q=−2​ln⁡(Ls+b/Lb)q=-2\ln(L_{s+b}/L_{b}) as defined in Sec. 3.8. Figure 6 shows the distributions of qq for the hypothesis of μ=0\mu=0 (background only) and μ=1\mu=1 (signal plus background) for the model described above using b=20b=20, s=10s=10 and τ=1\tau=1. The histograms are from Monte Carlo, and the solid curves are the predictions of the asymptotic formulae given in Sec. 3.8. Also shown are the pp-values for the background-only and signal-plus-background hypotheses corresponding to a possible observed value of the statistic qobsq_{\rm obs}.

5.1.1 Counting experiment with known bb

An important special case of the counting experiment above is where the mean background bb is known with negligible uncertainty and can be treated as a constant. This would correspond to having a very large value for the scale factor τ\tau.

If we regard bb as known, the data consist only of nn and thus the likelihood function is

L⁡(μ)=(μ​s+b)nn!​e−(μ​s+b),L(\mu)=\frac{(\mu s+b)^{n}}{n!}e^{-(\mu s+b)}\;, (98)

The test statistic for discovery q0q_{0} can be written

q0={−2​ln⁡L⁡(0)L⁡(μ^)μ^≥0,0μ^<0,q_{0}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}-2\ln\frac{L(0)}{L(\hat{\mu})}&\hat{\mu}\geq 0,\\[8.5359pt] 0&\hat{\mu}<0\;,\end{array}\right. (99)

where μ^=n−b\hat{\mu}=n-b. For sufficiently large bb we can use the asymptotic formula (55) for the significance,

Z0=q0={2​(n​ln⁡nb+b−n)μ^≥0,0μ^<0.Z_{0}=\sqrt{q_{0}}=\left\{\!\!\begin{array}[]{ll}\sqrt{2\left(n\ln\frac{n}{b}+b-n\right)}&\hat{\mu}\geq 0,\\[8.5359pt] 0&\hat{\mu}<0.\end{array}\right. (100)

To approximate the median significance assuming the nominal signal hypothesis (μ=1\mu=1) we replace nn by the Asimov value s+bs+b to obtain

med​[Z0|1]=q0,A=2​((s+b)​ln⁡(1+s/b)−s).\mbox{med}[Z_{0}|1]=\sqrt{q_{0,{\rm A}}}=\sqrt{2\left((s+b)\ln(1+s/b)-s\right)}\;. (101)

Expanding the logarithm in s/bs/b one finds

med​[Z0|1]=sb​(1+𝒪⁡(s/b)).\mbox{med}[Z_{0}|1]=\frac{s}{\sqrt{b}}\left(1+{\cal O}(s/b)\right)\;. (102)

Although Z0≈s/bZ_{0}\approx s/\sqrt{b} has been widely used for cases where s+bs+b is large, one sees here that this final approximation is strictly valid only for s≪bs\ll b.

Median values, assuming μ=1\mu=1, of Z0Z_{0} for different values of ss and bb are shown in Fig. 7. The solid curve shows Eq. (101), the dashed curve gives the approximation s/bs/\sqrt{b}, and the points are the exact median values from Monte Carlo. The structure seen in the points is due to the discrete nature of the data. One sees that Eq. (101) provides a much better approximation to the true median than does s/bs/\sqrt{b} in regions where s/bs/b cannot be regarded as small.

5.2 Shape Analysis

As a second example we consider the case where one is searching for a peak in an invariant mass distribution. The main histogram 𝐧=(n1,…,nN)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf n$}}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{N}) for background is shown in Fig. 8, which is here taken to be a Rayleigh distribution. The signal is modeled as a Gaussian of known width and mass (position). In this example there is no subsidiary histogram (m1,…,mM)(m_{1},\ldots,m_{M}).

If, as is often the case, the position of the peak is not known a priori, then one will test all masses in a given range, and appearance of a signal-like peak anywhere could lead to rejection of the background-only hypothesis. In such an analysis, however, the discovery significance must take into account the fact that a fluctuation could occur at any mass within the range. This is often referred to as the “look-elsewhere effect”, and is discussed further in Ref. [14].

In the example presented here, however, we will test all values of the mass and μ\mu using the statistic qμq_{\mu} for purposes of setting an upper limit on the signal strength. Here, each hypothesis of mass and signal strength is in effect tested individually, and thus the look-elsewhere effect does not come into play.

We assume that the signal and background distributions are known up to a scale factor. For the signal, this factor corresponds to the usual strength parameter μ\mu; for the background, we introduce an analogous factor θ\theta. That is, the mean value of the number of events in the iith bin is E⁡[ni]=μ​si+biE[n_{i}]=\mu s_{i}+b_{i}, where μ\mu is the signal strength parameter and the sis_{i} are taken as known. We assume that the background terms bib_{i} can be expressed as bi=θ​fb,ib_{i}=\theta f_{{\rm b},i}, where the probability to find a background event in bin ii, fb,if_{{\rm b},i}, is known, and θ\theta is a nuisance parameter that gives the total expected number of background events. Therefore the likelihood function can be written

L⁡(μ,θ)=∏i=1N(μ​si+θ​fb,i)nini!​e−(μ​si+θ​fb,i)L(\mu,\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{(\mu s_{i}+\theta f_{{\rm b},i})^{n_{i}}}{n_{i}!}e^{-(\mu s_{i}+\theta f_{{\rm b},i})} (103)

For a given data set 𝐧=(n1,…,nN)\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf n$}}=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{N}) one can evaluate the likelihood (103) and from this determine any of the test statistics discussed previously. Here we concentrate on the statistic qμq_{\mu} used to set an upper limit on μ\mu, and compare the distribution f⁡(qμ|μ′)f(q_{\mu}|\mu^{\prime}) from Eq.( 50) with histograms generated by Monte Carlo. Figure 9 shows f⁡(qμ|0)f(q_{\mu}|0) (red) and f⁡(qμ|μ)f(q_{\mu}|\mu) (blue).

The vertical line in Fig. 9 gives the median value of qμq_{\mu} assuming a strength parameter μ′=0\mu^{\prime}=0. The area to the right of this line under the curve of f⁡(qμ|μ)f(q_{\mu}|\mu) gives the pp-value of the hypothesized μ\mu, as shown shaded in green. The upper limit on μ\mu at a confidence level CL=1−α\mbox{CL}=1-\alpha is the value of μ\mu for which the pp-value is pμ=αp_{\mu}=\alpha. Figure 9 shows the distributions for the value of μ\mu that gave pμ=0.05p_{\mu}=0.05, corresponding to the 95% CL upper limit.

In addition to reporting the median limit, one would like to know how much it would vary for given statistical fluctuations in the data. This is illustrated in Fig. 10, which shows the same distributions as in Figure 9, but here the vertical line indicates the 15.87% quantile of the distribution f⁡(qμ|0)f(q_{\mu}|0), corresponding to having μ^\hat{\mu} fluctuate downward one standard deviation below its median.

By simulating the experiment many times with Monte Carlo, we can obtain a histogram of the upper limits on μ\mu at 95% CL, as shown in Fig. 11. The ±1​σ\pm 1\sigma (green) and ±2​σ\pm 2\sigma (yellow) error bands are obtained from the MC experiments. The vertical lines indicate the error bands as estimated directly (without Monte Carlo) using Eqs. (92) and (93). As can be seen from the plot, the agreement between the formulae and MC predictions is excellent.

Figures 9 through 11 correspond to finding upper limit on μ\mu for a specific value of the peak position (mass). In a search for a signal of unknown mass, the procedure would be repeated for all masses (in practice in small steps). Figure 12 shows the median upper limit at 95% CL as a function of mass. The median (central blue line) and error bands (±1​σ\pm 1\sigma in green, ±2​σ\pm 2\sigma in yellow) are obtained using Eqs. (92) and (93). The points and connecting curve correspond to the upper limit from a single arbitrary Monte Carlo data set, generated according to the background-only hypothesis. As can be seen, most of the plots lie as expected within the ±1​σ\pm 1\sigma error band.

6 Implementation in RooStats

Many of the results presented above are implemented or are being implemented in the RooStats framework [15], which is a C++ class library based on the ROOT [16] and RooFit [17] packages. The tools in RooStats can be used to represent arbitrary probability density functions that inherit from RooAbsPdf, the abstract interfaces for probability density functions provided by RooFit.

The framework provides an interface with minimization packages such as Minuit [18]. This allows one to obtain the estimators required in the the profile likelihood ratio: μ^\hat{\mu}, 𝜽^\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}, and 𝜽^^\hat{\hat{\mathchoice{\mbox{\boldmath$\displaystyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\textstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptstyle\bf\theta$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$\scriptscriptstyle\bf\theta$}}}}. The Asimov dataset defined in Eq. (24) can be determined for a probability density function by specifying the ExpectedData() command argument in a call to the generateBinned method. The Asimov data together with the standard HESSE covariance matrix provided by Minuit makes it is possible to determine the Fisher information matrix shown in Eq. (28), and thus obtain the related quantities such as the variance of μ^\hat{\mu} and the noncentrality parameter Λ\Lambda, which enter into the formulae for a number of the distributions of the test statistics presented above.

The distributions of the various test statistics and the related formulae for pp-values, sensitivities and confidence intervals as given in Sections 2, 3 and 4 are being incorporated as well. RooStats currently includes the test statistics tμt_{\mu}, t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu}, q0q_{0}, and qq, qμq_{\mu}, and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu} as concrete implementations of the TestStatistic interface. Together with the Asimov data, this provides the ability to calculate the alternative estimate, σA\sigma_{A}, for the variance of μ^\hat{\mu} shown in Eq. (30). The noncentral chi-square distribution is being incorporated into both RooStats and ROOT’s mathematics libraries for more general use. The various transformations of the noncentral chi-square used to obtain Eqs. (33), (41), (50), (57), and (3.7) are also in development in the form of concrete implementations of the SamplingDistribution interface. Together, these new classes will allow one to reproduce the examples shown in Section 5 and to extend them to an arbitrary model within the RooStats framework.

7 Conclusions

Statistical tests are described for use in planning and carrying out a search for new phenomena. The formalism allows for the treatment of systematic uncertainties through use of the profile likelihood ratio. Here a systematic uncertainty is included to the extent that the model includes a sufficient number of nuisance parameters so that for at least some point in its parameter space it can be regarded as true.

Approximate formulae are given for the distributions of test statistics used to characterize the level of agreement between the data and the hypothesis being tested, as well as the related expressions for pp-values and significances. The statistics are based on the profile likelihood ratio and can be used for a two-sided test of a strength parameter μ\mu (tμt_{\mu}), a one-sided test for discovery (q0q_{0}), and a one-sided test for finding an upper limit (qμq_{\mu} and q~μ\tilde{q}_{\mu}). The statistic t~μ\tilde{t}_{\mu} can be used to obtain a “unified” confidence interval, in the sense that it is one- or two-sided depending on the data outcome.

Formulae are also given that allow one to characterize the sensitivity of a planned experiment through the median significance of a given hypothesis under assumption of a different one, e.g., median significance with which one would reject the background-only hypothesis under assumption of a certain signal model. These exploit the use of an artificial data set, the “Asimov” data set, defined so as to make estimators for all parameters equal to their true values. Methods for finding the expected statistical variation in the sensitivity (error bands) are also given.

These tools free one from the need to carry out lengthy Monte Carlo calculations, which in the case of a discovery at 5​σ5\sigma significance could require simulation of around 10810^{8} measurements. They are are particularly useful in cases where one needs to estimate experimental sensitivities for many points in a multidimensional parameter space (e.g., for models such as supersymmetry), which would require generating a large MC sample for each point.

The approximations used are valid in the limit of a large data sample. Tests with Monte Carlo indicate, however, that the formulae are in fact reasonably accurate even for fairly small samples, and thus can have a wide range of practical applicability. For very small samples and in cases where high accuracy is crucial, one is always free to validate the approximations with Monte Carlo.
